problem.text: What is the remainder when $12^{2011}+11^{2012}$ is divided by seven?

steps.title: Where to start: huge exponents, prime modulus
steps.body:
The exponents are far too big to compute, but we only need a remainder mod $7$, and $7$ is prime. Fermat's little theorem says: if $p$ is prime and $p$ does not divide $a$, then $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$. Neither $12$ nor $11$ is a multiple of $7$, so both satisfy
$$12^6 \equiv 1 \pmod 7, \qquad 11^6 \equiv 1 \pmod 7.$$

your_turn.prompt: Reduce the bases: what are $12$ and $11$ modulo $7$?

steps.title: Split the exponents into blocks of 6
steps.body: Since a sixth power gives $1$, only the remainder of each exponent after dividing by $6$ matters. Write each exponent as a multiple of $6$ plus a small leftover.

your_turn.prompt: Find the remainders when $2011$ and $2012$ are divided by $6$.
your_turn.answer: $2011 = 6\cdot 335 + 1$ and $2012 = 6\cdot 335 + 2$, so the remainders are $1$ and $2$.

your_turn.prompt: Write $11^{2012}$ in the same way, as a power of $11^6$ times something.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: So $11^{2012} \equiv 11^2 \equiv 4^2 = 16 \equiv 2 \pmod 7$. Adding, $12^{2011} + 11^{2012} \equiv 5 + 2 = 7 \equiv 0 \pmod 7$. The sum is a multiple of $7$, and the remainder is **$0$**.
